articles.title: In 2021, Spain tested steelmaking slag in a porous road; after 3 years, the surface had no visible damage and its grip reading stayed above 70
articles.summary: Discover how Spain's trial of porous asphalt containing steelmaking slag has proven effective after three years, with no visible damage and maintained skid resistance. Learn about the implications for road construction and sustainability!
articles.body: A road surface that was built with waste from steelmaking was still in good condition after three years of use in Spain, with the project using porous asphalt that contained up to 10% ladle furnace slag, a by-product of steel production. Trial measurements found that the surface retained a skid-resistance score above 70, while visual inspections found no significant damage.The findings are a result of a field study published in Case Studies in Construction Materials in July 2025, which reported that the mixture could be manufactured and compacted on a full-scale test section after earlier laboratory work. The trial covered a parking area and a two-lane road, and a thin layer of porous asphalt was placed over existing pavement.The surface kept its grip during the trialA good measure of how resistant a road surface is to slipping is skid resistance, and the researchers used the British Pendulum Number, or BPN, to assess the pavement's friction. The readings were consistently above 70 during the monitoring period, including the final measurements that were taken in 2024.Testing took place more frequently during the first year and continued at six-month intervals as the pavement aged, with the final readings showing that the surface was able to maintain good skid resistance over the three-year period. The researchers also assessed the pavement's durability under conditions that included moisture, frost, abrasion and ageing, and the results met the requirements considered suitable for urban roads carrying medium levels of heavy traffic, according to the full research paper published in Case Studies in Construction Materials.The road still had a drainage issue to manageThe purpose of porous asphalt is to let water pass through its connected gaps, and that drainage performance can change if dust and loose material collect on the surface, even if the pavement remains structurally sound. In the Spanish trial, it was found that the central part of the road and the parking area retained their drainage capacity relatively well, but sections near the road's beginning and end experienced more clogging, which the researchers attributed to loose material that was carried in from nearby areas.The permeability remained above the minimum levels that were discussed by the researchers for the pavement's intended use, despite those changes. The findings show why road performance cannot be judged by surface appearance or grip alone, since drainage also needs to be measured over time.The material could reduce demand for conventional inputsLadle furnace slag is usually generated during the production of steel, and using it in asphalt could be a potential way to reuse an industrial by-product instead of having to completely rely on conventional materials. The research team tested a mixture that contained up to 10% slag without needing preliminary physical or chemical treatment of the material. Could substances leach out of the mixture? The reported results remained below the applicable regulatory limits, and that finding is important to the assessment of whether industrial by-products can be used in road construction, although it applies to the material and conditions examined in this trial.The researchers stated that the pilot was successful, right from laboratory design to road construction and field monitoring, but three years of observations do not establish how the surface will perform over the full life of a road. The paper pushes for longer monitoring periods, which could potentially span 10 to 20 years, as a useful next step.Currently, the trial provides field evidence that porous asphalt that has ladle furnace slag can maintain skid resistance and an acceptable surface condition over several years. Its long-term durability and drainage performance will need further observation before the results can be applied more widely.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In a 1986 field test, engineers added tiny vortex generators to turbine blades; annual energy output rose nearly 6% at one test site
articles.summary: Explore how tiny vortex generators enhanced wind turbine blade performance, increasing energy output by almost 6% in a pivotal 1986 field test. Discover the impact of design on wind energy efficiency.
articles.body: A wind turbine blade works like an aviation wing. For the blade to provide lift and continue rotating, air must flow smoothly over its curved surface. When that smooth flow separates from the surface, lift decreases, drag increases, and the turbine wastes wind that could have been converted into power. For decades, engineers have struggled with this issue, and one of the least expensive solutions is also one of the smallest. To alter the way air behaves as it passes, tiny fins that are only a small portion of the blade's width can be adhered to the surface in tidy rows. Wind energy has a surprisingly lengthy history with what are known as vortex generators.A NASA contractor study dated July 1986 gave some actual data on that history. The paper was written by G. W. Gyatt of the California company AeroVironment and reported on field experiments of vortex generators on a tiny turbine dubbed the Carter Model 25. The fins covered the full blade, and at one test site energy output increased by about 6% annually. That sounds humble. But it was off an inexpensive add-on and was measured on a real machine in actual wind, not on a computer model.Why little fins are goodA vortex generator is a tiny vane that is angled to the oncoming air. The fin makes a little whirlpool when the wind blows past it. This whirlpool is called a vortex. That swirl draws faster-moving air down into the slow, sticky stuff that's clinging to the blade, and the electrified layer stays around longer before the airflow separates and the blade stalls. Wind engineers borrowed the trick, which was first devised to delay stall on aeroplane wings.There is another reason turbine blades can benefit from vortex generators. Insects, dust and grime collect on the leading edge and roughen the surface, disrupting the smooth flow the blade was supposed to have. The 1986 team went straight to the test and added roughness strips to simulate bug and dirt buildup and checked to see if the fins would mitigate the damage. They did. A dirty leading edge was a performance killer, but the fins more than made up for that. A wonderful bonus for blades that spend years outside.What the 1986 test revealedThe Carter Model 25 was a tiny machine with a rotor of around 32 ft (9.8 m) in diameter. The engineers tested the fins in three configurations: on the inner half of each blade, on the outer half and over the whole length. The fins were paired, and the vortices were rotated in opposite directions. Each was four times as long as high, and its height was barely half to one percent of the breadth of the blade.The results varied with wind speed. Above about 10 metres per second (22 miles per hour), the fins increased power output by as much as 20%; at lower wind speeds, they caused a performance penalty of less than 4%. That penalty did not necessarily cancel out the gains over an entire year, because annual energy production reflects performance across the site's full range of wind conditions. Fins on the outer half of the blade performed better than those on the inner half. The full-span configuration increased annual energy output by nearly 6% at a site with an average wind speed of 16 miles per hour (about 7.2 metres per second).There were other ways to change the power curve. The 1986 team noted that increasing the blade pitch angle could produce a similar effect. Vortex generators had another advantage: they reduced performance losses caused by dirt and insects accumulating along the blade's leading edge. Their use on wind turbines dated to 1983, when they were tested on the much larger Boeing MOD-2 machine, increasing annual energy production by 11% to 15%. Results from that earlier test were subsequently scaled to develop the configuration used on the Carter Model 25, as a 1996 NREL review explains.Where the profits end upThe aerodynamics of the MOD 2 blades were less than optimal; therefore, there remained space for improvement. Other turbine designs may gain less from vortex generators, depending on their blade geometry and sensitivity to surface roughness. A separate NREL-funded project in the mid-1990s tested vortex generators on the AWT-26, a two-bladed turbine with a 26.2-metre rotor. Although the fins increased power output at moderate wind speeds, drag reduced output at lower speeds enough to produce a net decline in annual energy at sites with average wind speeds up to 8.5 metres per second (about 19 miles per hour), according to NREL's report.Newer evidence, with careful placement of the fins, looks more promising. In a 2020 study in the journal Wind Energy, which can be seen on the research portal of DTU, the Technical University of Denmark, fins were evaluated on megawatt-scale turbines affected by surface roughness. Over 27 months, six turbines were involved, three of which had fins, and each had a neighbour as a reference. All three installed turbines produced more energy afterwards, with the average gain being 3.3% compared to the 2.8% projected by the authors' model.The researchers also warned that vortex generators placed in the wrong part of a blade, or designed too large or too far out, can reduce annual energy production. Engineering modelling is therefore necessary before the devices are installed on a specific turbine, because their effects depend on blade design, surface condition and the local wind regime. Vortex generators can improve airflow over turbine blades, but their effectiveness depends on the blade design, surface condition and local wind regime. The Carter Model 25 test and later trials show that gains at some wind speeds can be offset by added drag at others. Careful modelling and site-specific testing are therefore essential before fitting the devices to an existing turbine.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2021, a Texas city moved to take Jim Burgess’ 3.548-acre property after a $1.1 million purchase effort failed; five years later, the state Supreme Court will decide if it can be condemned for a private golf facility
articles.summary: The Texas Supreme Court has agreed to hear a dispute over whether a local government can take private property through eminent domain to build a golf
articles.body: The Texas Supreme Court has agreed to hear a dispute over whether a local government can take private property through eminent domain to build a golf facility that will be leased to a private operator. The case involves a 3.548-acre plot of land in Westworth Village owned by local resident Jim Burgess. In 2021, city officials tried to buy the property for $1.1 million as part of a larger plan to redevelop the municipal golf course, Hawk’s Creek. After Mr Burgess rejected the offer, the city moved to take the land through eminent domain, a legal process that allows the government to acquire private property without the owner's consent. Five years after the dispute began, justices on the state's highest court will consider whether local governments have the constitutional power to take private land for projects intended to be run by private businesses.Early legal actions and initial valuationAfter the city council moved to take the property, Mr Burgess filed a legal challenge against Westworth Village. Records from the Second Court of Appeals of Texas show that a trial court first appointed three special commissioners to decide how much the land was worth. The panel valued the property at $1.545 million. Mr Burgess challenged the valuation in trial court. The court rejected his argument that the taking itself was unlawful, but the dispute over compensation continued to a jury trial. The jury eventually awarded him $1.3 million under state laws governing eminent domain. Mr Burgess was unhappy with the decision allowing the city to take his land, so he appealed the condemnation order to the Second Court of Appeals in Fort Worth. At the same time, Westworth Village appealed a separate order requiring the city to pay court costs.Appeals court overturns land seizureOn 19 June 2025, a three-judge panel of the appeals court, made up of Justices Mike Wallach, Elizabeth Kerr and Brian Walker, ruled in favour of Mr Burgess. Justice Wallach wrote the majority opinion, which overturned the trial court's decision and sent the case back for further proceedings. The ruling said that state laws and constitutional rules place strict limits on how local governments can use eminent domain. The court reviewed city plans showing that the land was meant to become part of a leased facility called the Golf Performance Center at Hawk's Creek. Under the lease documents, the facility would include a driving range, practice areas, a clubhouse, parking facilities and an office.Justice Wallach stressed that Texas courts must carefully examine cases in which local governments try to force owners to sell their property. “These circumstances help explain why our law directs Texas courts to carefully scrutinize any exercise of eminent-domain authority,” wrote Justice Wallach. “Condemnation is one area in which the government must turn sharp corners. It is a fit role for the judiciary to ensure that the government stays in its lane.”Lawyers representing Mr Burgess at Johnston Tobey Baruch welcomed the appeals court's decision. “We are delighted with the court's ruling, which will permit our client to continue his challenge to the taking in the trial court,” the firm stated after the ruling.Constitutional limits and arguments over public useThe main legal question concerns Article I, Section 17 of the Texas Constitution. It states that private property cannot be taken or used for public purposes without proper compensation. Changes to state law and constitutional amendments introduced in 2005, including Chapter 2206 of the Texas Government Code, also place clear limits on government use of eminent domain. These rules prohibit taking private property for economic development or transferring it to private entities, subject to the law's specific provisions. Westworth Village officials argued that taking the 3.548-acre plot qualified as public use because it would become part of a park and golf course redevelopment project open to the public. However, the appeals court said that the legal definition of public parks cannot override constitutional protections against forced property transfers that benefit private operators. Legal observers say the case will test the limits between public leisure facilities and unlawful transfers of land to private businesses. Local governments regularly run public parks, but allowing private companies to operate facilities built on land taken through eminent domain raises difficult legal questions under Texas law.Final review by state supreme courtAfter losing in the appeals court, Westworth Village asked the Supreme Court of Texas to review the decision. According to court records, the state Supreme Court granted review on 2 October 2026 under case number 25-0836. Oral arguments before the state Supreme Court justices are scheduled for 11 January 2027. The court's decision is expected to set a binding legal precedent across Texas on whether local governments can use eminent domain to acquire land for municipal sports facilities that are operated by commercial businesses.You use AI every day. articles.title: n 1997, Alabama sank 124 obsolete voting machines to create a 1.5-mile artificial reef lane; officials said the 830-pound units remained intact
articles.summary: In a creative marine conservation effort, Alabama sunk 124 obsolete voting machines to create a 1.5-mile artificial reef that has flourished into a feeding ground for mackerel and other fish species. Learn about the significance of this unique project for marine life and local fisheries.
articles.body: The majority of the sand on the bottom along Alabama's Gulf coast is flat. Red snapper and many other reef fish require hard structure to survive; therefore, this is bad news for fish that need a place to hide and feed. The state and local fishing groups have sunk objects as a fairly practical solution to the issue throughout the years. Fish have taken up residence in car bodies, concrete culverts, bridge debris, barges, and even military tanks. When a lengthy row of outdated voting machines was placed across the bottom in October 1997, one of the strangest undertakings was completed.Alabama’s artificial reef program dates to 1953, when the Orange Beach Charter Boat Association sought permission to place 250 car bodies off Baldwin County. The voting-machine project was a later, more targeted effort intended to establish a trolling lane for nearshore king and Spanish mackerel.Why the seabed needed helpMuch of Alabama’s offshore seabed consists of flat sand, which offers limited hard structure for reef fish. Adding vertical surfaces can attract species such as snappers and groupers. Over time, corals and sponges colonise the submerged material, smaller animals take up residence, and larger fish arrive to feed. With sufficient time, an artificial reef can develop a food web resembling that of a natural reef, according to the state’s artificial reef guidance. That's why an uncommon substance, a voting machine, can work. What matters is that it protrudes from the sand, provides cover and attracts smaller fish to feed on. These also were heavy things, 830 pounds a piece.Formation of the ReefThe idea came from Iris Ethridge, a retired captain and former schoolteacher from Orange Beach, who wanted to establish a nearshore trolling lane for king and Spanish mackerel, according to Alabama Outdoor News. She figured if there was a trolling alley for mackerel close to shore, the tiny boats and the big vessels could catch them. Her search for reef material turned up 124 outdated voting machines weighing 830 pounds each. Together, the machines weighed 102,920 pounds, or about 51.5 U.S. short tons (46.7 metric tonnes). Then she collaborated with the late Vernon Minton, long-time director of the state’s Marine Resources Division, on a layout.The devices were wired up in groups of four, which constituted 31 clusters, and strung out in a single line 1.5 miles, or around 2.4 kilometres, long. The line stretched between two existing reefs: the sunken Liberty ship Allen and the Bridge Rubble Reef, an artificial reef made from bridge debris. The troll alley was completed in October 1997. This provided the boats with a continuous passage from one established reef to the other. Some bridge rubble, concrete and huge rocks were also placed along the line by crews.Alabama Outdoor News quoted Minton as saying the crew was surprised by how well the machines remained intact after deployment. The structures formed part of a trolling lane designed to provide habitat and feeding opportunities for king mackerel between two existing reefs. Alabama has employed objects such as voting machines, concrete, barges and Liberty ships, according to a 2016 summary of Gulf reef projects from Texas Parks & Wildlife, hosted by NOAA Fisheries. The reef performed what it was supposed to do, but also raises a reasonable issue as to what such efforts actually show.The voice of the reefThe voting machine lane makes a good narrative, but the overall picture is fish and money. In testimony before the House Natural Resources Committee in 2013, Chris Blankenship, then head of the Alabama Marine Resources Division, stated the state has seeded more than 17,000 reefs in its reef zone, which includes about 1,200 square miles of federal waters. That ecosystem produces a fishery for red snapper that averages around 30% of the Gulf’s recreationally captured red snapper from less than 5% of its shoreline, he said.There should be a word of warning here, too. An issue across all the Gulf states in the same 2016 assessment is a need for increased scientific understanding of reef biology and design. Reefs are undoubtedly attractive to fish, but showing how much they contribute to the total population calls for meticulous long-term monitoring. Minton’s account describes the machines remaining intact and forming structures along which king mackerel could feed. It does not establish how quickly fish began using the structures or measure the lane’s long-term ecological effects.To summarise, Alabama converted 124 old voting machines, approximately 46.7 tonnes of equipment, into a reef lane of 1.5 miles between two existing reefs, in October 1997. State officials stated the equipment was holding up well and they had king mackerel spots to feed. The project illustrates the conversion of a flat sandy bottom into a fishing ground with whatever stout material is at hand. The long-term fish benefits of any one reef are best determined by diligent observation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘What's the need for SSR?’ Akhilesh Yadav says BJP conspiring to add fake votes, urges SP workers to be vigilant
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday accused the BJP of conspiring to manipulate electoral rolls by adding bogus votes and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday accused the BJP of conspiring to manipulate electoral rolls by adding bogus votes and deleting genuine votes of opposition supporters, urging party workers to remain vigilant at their respective polling booths ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.Addressing party leaders and workers from various districts at the SP headquarters in Lucknow, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister alleged that the BJP was resorting to electoral malpractice to win elections and disregarding the Constitution.In a statement released by the party, Yadav said, "BJP is conspiring to add fake votes to electoral rolls. Party workers should remain vigilant at their respective polling booths. The BJP considers fake votes and dishonesty its strength. It resorts to different types of electoral manoeuvres, including getting fake votes added to electoral rolls and genuine votes of opposition parties deleted."He urged people to remain alert against what he described as "vote theft and donation theft".Yadav raises concerns over electoral roll revisionsYadav's allegations come days after he questioned the rationale behind the Election Commission's Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls.He had said the Samajwadi Party was not opposed to either the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) or SSR, but would resist any alleged attempt to manipulate voter lists to benefit the BJP."When the Election Commission of India spent thousands of crores of rupees and completed the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls a couple of months ago, what is the need for SSR?" Yadav had asked.He also alleged that complaints about irregularities in electoral rolls had not resulted in punitive action, despite what he described as documentary evidence. During the news conference,Yadav presented a man named Vikas Yadav, claiming that his name appeared at 12 different places on the electoral rolls.The SP chief also said the party had deployed PDA praharis to assist voters with the revision exercise at the booth level.BJP accused of failing on governanceApart from electoral issues, Yadav criticised the BJP government's record in Uttar Pradesh, citing inflation, unemployment, corruption, alleged misuse of public funds, injustice and atrocities as concerns affecting people.He accused the ruling party of protecting land grabbers and alleged that people associated with the BJP were encroaching on land belonging to poor and vulnerable sections of society, as well as government land.Yadav further claimed that people approaching authorities for justice were being implicated in cases and that the police often sided with influential BJP supporters.He asserted that public support for a Samajwadi Party government was growing and expressed confidence that voters would hold the BJP accountable in the 2027 Assembly elections."Once the BJP is removed from power in 2027, it will never return," Yadav said.He also claimed that the PDA community, referring to Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak (backward classes, Dalits and minorities), was united and alleged that the BJP government and the chief minister were targeting its members because of their unity.Education system and examination leaks flaggedYadav accused the BJP government of weakening Uttar Pradesh's education system, claiming that more than 26,000 primary schools had been shut down over the past decade while the number of liquor shops had increased.He alleged that corruption and exploitation had harmed school education and that teachers, educational institutions, graduates and young people faced discrimination.The SP chief also claimed that Uttar Pradesh had recorded the highest number of examination paper leaks in the country, accusing the state government of failing to ensure the integrity of recruitment and other examinations.In his earlier remarks, Yadav had also alleged that concerns over voter-list manipulation extended across generations, saying that young people were raising questions about the electoral process.He additionally criticised the BJP's proposed 'One Nation, One Election' plan, alleging that it could allow the party to consolidate control over governments across the country and avoid accountability through repeated elections.Yadav maintained that the BJP had little to show for its time in office and accused its leadership of wasting time in government.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Refrain from taking photos, take shelter': India advisory amid Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Sunday issued an advisory for its citizens in Saudi Arabia, urging them to follow revised emergency safety guidelines issued by local
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Sunday issued an advisory for its citizens in Saudi Arabia, urging them to follow revised emergency safety guidelines issued by local authorities amid heightened security concerns following drone and missile attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels.The Indian mission in Riyadh advised citizens to remain inside their homes or residential buildings until the threat subsides, keep away from open spaces, windows and glass structures, and avoid standing on balconies or rooftops.The guidelines urge people to remain calm and move quickly to the nearest safe location inside a building, preferably an internal room away from windows and glass fixtures, until the danger has passed.Those outdoors have been advised to enter the nearest building or take shelter behind a sturdy obstacle. They have also been asked to avoid large gatherings and hazardous areas and refrain from taking photographs.Motorists who receive an alert while driving have been advised to pull over safely, keeping away from overpasses and elevated structures.In case of an imminent threat or emergency, Indian citizens can dial 911 in Makkah, Madinah, Riyadh and the Eastern Province, and 998 in other parts of Saudi Arabia, according to the guidelines.The mission has also urged Indian nationals to follow instructions issued by authorised Saudi authorities through official communication channels.The advisory comes amid heightened security concerns following drone and missile attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels targeting Saudi territory, including a deadly strike at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10.The attack killed an Indian national and injured several others, prompting the Indian diplomatic mission to reiterate precautionary measures.Following the October 10 strike, the embassy had urged Indian nationals to follow local authorities' instructions, remain indoors during aerial attacks and refrain from filming, publishing or sharing information, photographs or videos related to the ongoing events.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Check CCTV, I am innocent': Wanted model Shraddha Dubey breaks silence, claims businessman died by suicide in video
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Model and socialite Shraddha Dubey, who is wanted in connection with the death of restaurant owner Shiva Sharma, on Sunday issued her first
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Model and socialite Shraddha Dubey, who is wanted in connection with the death of restaurant owner Shiva Sharma, on Sunday issued her first public statement to a news agency denying all allegations of murder and claiming that Sharma died by suicide after jumping from the fourth floor of her apartment building.Her statement came as Lucknow Police increased the reward for information leading to the arrest of Shraddha, her sister Rashmi Dubey and their driver from Rs 25,000 to Rs 50,000 each. While, she still remains elusive.In a video statement, Shraddha maintained that she was innocent and urged the police to examine CCTV footage from her apartment building, claiming it would establish her innocence.She questioned why investigators had examined CCTV footage near the Nepal border but had not, according to her, retrieved footage from her building.“If the CCTV cameras in my building are examined, I will be proved innocent. I have done nothing,” she said, rejecting the allegations against her.Shraddha claimed that she had known Sharma for only four months, during which they were friends for around two-and-a-half months. She said he had started visiting her home regularly only during the last two months of their association.She also alleged that Sharma's mother had never approved of their relationship, partly because Shraddha was around 12 years older than him. She claimed the accusations against her were motivated by this hostility.In her statement, Shraddha said Sharma had told her that he was under financial pressure and owed approximately Rs 16–17 lakh. According to her, he had also asked her for financial assistance.She further claimed that Sharma had taken jewellery worth approximately Rs 5–6 lakh from her home about a month before his death. However, she described the matter as a personal issue and said Sharma had acknowledged taking the jewellery in a video and promised to return it.Shraddha said she left the apartment because she was experiencing breathing difficulties and was emotionally distressed. She claimed she had wanted to face the situation but became frightened after her driver was allegedly assaulted and accusations of murder were levelled against her.She also defended her sister Rashmi, saying she had visited her after a long time and had no connection with Sharma. Shraddha alleged that her sister had been unnecessarily implicated in the case.Denying any connection with other people whose photographs with her had circulated, she said photographs alone did not establish involvement in a crime.Appealing to the police and the judiciary, Shraddha called for an impartial investigation and said no one should be branded a criminal before the allegations were established.“I request the police and the judiciary to ensure a fair investigation. Accusing someone of murder and portraying them as a criminal across the country is not justice,” she said.Shraddha, her sister Rashmi and their driver remain wanted in connection with Sharma's death. Police have increased the reward to Rs 50,000 each for information leading to their arrest, as efforts to trace them continue.Sharma died on October 9 after falling from the fourth floor of an apartment in Lucknow's Hazratganj area. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death. articles.title: Brazilian man sells all his belongings and travels 1,200 miles to meet online girlfriend he hoped to marry, only to discover she was an AI-generated farm girl seeking a partner
articles.summary: A Brazilian man who sold all his belongings and travelled more than 1,200 miles to meet the woman he hoped to marry was left heartbroken after discovering
articles.body: A Brazilian man who sold all his belongings and travelled more than 1,200 miles to meet the woman he hoped to marry was left heartbroken after discovering that his online girlfriend was an artificial intelligence-generated character.Edimar Martins, 49, a bricklayer from Maranhao in northeastern Brazil, told local broadcaster TV Mirante that he first came across a social media profile featuring a woman named Jessica Oliveira in 2020. Believing she was real, Martins eventually decided to travel to meet the woman he had fallen for online.Brazilian man sells everything to meet his AI girlfriendAccording to Martins, he sold his personal belongings on October 9 to pay for a bus journey to Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais in southeastern Brazil. He arrived in the city on October 11, hoping to finally meet the woman he believed could be his life partner.“I sold all my things, I got rid of everything,” Martins said, reflecting on the sacrifices he had made for the journey. “That’s how you get discouraged, who wouldn’t get discouraged?”However, his hopes were shattered when he failed to locate the woman. Martins eventually approached a local radio station for help, only to be told that the woman he was searching for did not exist.“I went to the radio station there, and they said no, that’s fake news, that woman doesn’t exist,” he said.AI-generated woman promised to support him financiallyThe woman Martins believed he was going to meet appeared in videos shared through a TikTok account that reportedly had around 300,000 followers. The account, @JessicaFazendeira, featured an AI-generated persona who presented herself as a woman looking for a partner to live with her on her farm.In one video that was later deleted, the character claimed she wanted a man she could welcome to her property and support financially, promising that he would no longer have to work.“I really want to support you, I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life,” the AI-generated character said in the video.The promise appears to have contributed to the impression that the woman was genuine. However, the person behind the account later acknowledged that the character was created using artificial intelligence and denied having any direct communication with Martins.Person behind TikTok account admits character was created using AIIn a video posted on Wednesday, the person responsible for the account addressed the controversy and clarified that the woman featured in the videos was not real.“I came here to state the obvious: I am made of artificial intelligence,” the character said in the video.The person behind the account also denied personally speaking to Martins or inviting him to travel to Belo Horizonte.“I have never spoken to anyone with this profile. The intention was to gain engagement for sale,” the statement read.“I never spoke directly to anyone, much less took anyone to Belo Horizonte. It was a surprise to me to see what is happening.”The revelation left Martins facing not only emotional disappointment but also financial hardship after spending the money he had raised by selling his possessions on the journey.Man receives assistance to return home after running out of moneyAfter failing to find the woman and eventually running out of money, Martins approached Belo Horizonte City Hall. He reportedly spoke to a social worker and explained that he had travelled a long distance in search of love because he was tired of being alone.He subsequently received assistance to return home.Speaking about his experience, Martins described the emotional toll of the incident and the disappointment of believing he had found a partner, only to discover that the relationship was based on an AI-generated identity.“It only brings sadness, discouragement, depression. Many people wanted to find a relationship, so I came,” he said.Despite the setback, Martins has not given up on finding a romantic partner. He is currently staying with a family member and has expressed his determination to return to Belo Horizonte in the hope of meeting someone with whom he can build a future.“I didn’t find her, but I’ll find another one, and it will be in the same place I went, and I’ll go again,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Woman evicted after bitter neighbour dispute over shared driveway loses High Court fight to stop sale of her home over unpaid debts and legal costs
articles.summary: The High Court has ruled that the sale of a woman’s home can proceed after she was evicted following a long-running dispute with her neighbour over a
articles.body: The High Court has ruled that the sale of a woman’s home can proceed after she was evicted following a long-running dispute with her neighbour over a shared driveway. In a judgment handed down on 16 March 2026, the court upheld an earlier order allowing the property to be sold to recover unpaid damages and legal costs. The case, Kirsten Elaine McGowan v Marie Bernadette Potter [2026], concerned whether the County Court had the legal authority to order the sale. The ruling confirmed that the original order was valid, leaving Potter’s challenge unsuccessful on the preliminary issues considered by the High Court.How did a driveway dispute leave a woman £69,351 in debtAccording to the High Court judgment, the proceedings arose from an earlier legal dispute between Kirsten Elaine McGowan and Marie Bernadette Potter over a shared driveway. On 26 August 2020, an order required Potter to pay McGowan £30,452.95 in damages, together with £27,000 in legal costs. Potter did not pay the sums awarded, and the amount owed continued to increase as interest accrued and further legal costs were incurred.The judgment described the case as “yet another cautionary tale about the financial consequences of neighbour disputes for those without deep pockets”. On 30 December 2020, the County Court Money Claims Centre made a final charging order against Potter’s property at 25 Bennetts Avenue, Shirley, in Croydon. The order was for £69,351.07, and the judgment noted that there had been no appeal against it. A charging order allows a creditor to secure a debt against a debtor’s property, potentially enabling the property to be sold to recover the outstanding money.Why was a woman evicted over a £77,373 debtMcGowan applied to the County Court at Croydon in May 2021 for an order to proceed with the sale of Potter’s home. Following a hearing in December 2021, the court made an order dated 29 December, subsequently varied in January 2022. It provided that the sale would not proceed if Potter paid £77,373.56 by 28 January 2022. The order also required the property to be sold for no less than £575,000, although the minimum sale price was reduced later.The order further required Potter to provide vacant possession of the property by 25 February 2022. To facilitate the sale, it provided for a legal term of 3,000 years to be created and vested in McGowan under section 90 of the Law of Property Act 1925. Potter did not give possession as required. A warrant for possession was enforced on 26 April 2023, resulting in her eviction. At the time of the High Court proceedings, the property had not been sold, and the outstanding debt remained unpaid.Why did a woman challenge a home sale order over a £30,000 legal limitIn October 2024, Potter challenged the County Court order because it had been made beyond the court’s legal powers. McGowan subsequently brought proceedings in the High Court on 23 December 2024, seeking an order under the Law of Property Act 1925 to create and vest the 3,000-year legal term needed to enforce the sale order. The proceedings focused on whether the County Court had jurisdiction to make the original order and, if it did not, whether that would render the order invalid.The dispute centred on the financial limits governing the County Court’s authority to enforce charging orders and make associated orders under the 1925 Act. Potter argued that the County Court’s powers under sections 90 and 91 were restricted to cases involving debts of no more than £30,000. McGowan’s case was that the relevant limit was the County Court’s wider equity jurisdiction, which had been increased to £350,000. The High Court considered the relationship between these provisions before determining whether the original sale order had been lawfully made.Why the High Court upheld the sale of a woman’s homeIn his judgment dated 16 March 2026, Mr David Halpern KC, sitting as a High Court judge, rejected Potter’s argument that the County Court lacked the necessary jurisdiction. He concluded that the authority to enforce charging orders through a sale fell within the County Court’s equity jurisdiction, subject to a limit of £350,000. The court therefore found that the original order had been validly made.The judge explained that the powers under sections 90 and 91 of the Law of Property Act 1925 supported the court’s jurisdiction to enforce charging orders through a sale. He concluded that those powers were subject to the same £350,000 limit rather than a separate £30,000 restriction. The judgment stated: “The Order was therefore validly made.” This finding resolved the preliminary jurisdiction issue in McGowan’s favour and rejected the central legal argument underpinning Potter’s challenge.The High Court also addressed the legal consequences that would have followed had the County Court exceeded its jurisdiction. The judge explained that, even if the original order had been made without jurisdiction, it would not automatically have become a nullity that could simply be ignored. Instead, it would remain binding unless and until it was set aside by a court. However, because he found that the County Court had the necessary authority, this alternative issue did not change the outcome of the case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Pakistan plans Moon landing by 2035, expands space cooperation with China
articles.summary: Pakistan aims to land on the Moon by 2035 as it expands its space programme, planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday, announcing that the country's
articles.body: Pakistan aims to land on the Moon by 2035 as it expands its space programme, planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday, announcing that the country's first astronaut would embark on a space mission from China on November 25.Addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week 2026 in Narowal district of Punjab province, Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions.Pakistan’s “first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China’s space centre on November 25, while the country aims to achieve a lunar landing by 2035,” he said, according to news agency PTI.The minister highlighted the growing role of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security. He stressed that scientific research and space exploration were important for technological advancement.First Pakistani astronaut to travel to China’s space stationThe upcoming mission is part of wider cooperation between Pakistan and China in space science and technology. According to Reuters, two Pakistani candidates, pilots Khurram Daud and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, have been undergoing training in China, with one expected to be selected for the flight.The selected astronaut will serve as a payload specialist aboard China's Tiangong space station, conducting scientific experiments rather than operating the spacecraft, Reuters reported last month.Pakistan's space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), signed an agreement with the China Manned Space Agency in February 2025 to prepare a Pakistani astronaut for the mission, according to The Express Tribune.The two candidates had been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing, learning spacecraft systems, Mandarin and the physical demands of spaceflight.The mission is expected to last about a week. The astronaut will travel aboard a Chinese spacecraft launched from China and return to Earth with members of a Chinese crew.Pakistan does not have an independent launch vehicle or crewed spacecraft, making the mission dependent on China's space infrastructure and training facilities.Pakistan-China cooperation extends to lunar explorationBeyond the human spaceflight programme, Pakistan and China are collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover planned for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028.The rover is intended to use artificial intelligence-based stereo imaging to identify obstacles, assess distances and navigate the lunar surface autonomously, as direct real-time control from Earth would not be possible.However, Pakistan's participation in the lunar rover project is separate from its stated ambition to land on the Moon by 2035.According to Reuters, a Pakistani space agency official last month had said there was no official commitment or discussion about sending a Pakistani astronaut to the Moon under the existing partnership.Space education and proposed museumIqbal was speaking at the conclusion of World Space Week 2026, which was celebrated in Narowal for the first time in collaboration with SUPARCO. The event aimed to raise awareness among young people about space science, scientific research and modern technology.The minister also announced plans to establish Pakistan's first Space Museum at the University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness and encourage students to pursue careers in space science and technology.He said improved access to higher education was allowing students who had previously faced financial barriers to perform well academically.Iqbal congratulated the University of Narowal on securing first position at the Islamabad Science Festival, saying the achievement reflected the talent and potential of Pakistan's youth.The minister said the proposed museum would further encourage young people to explore scientific fields and pursue opportunities in space research and technology.India’s space roadmap: From Gaganyaan to a Moon landingIndia has also been advancing its space programme, with plans to send astronauts into orbit, establish its own space station and land an Indian on the Moon by 2040.According to the Union government’s roadmap outlined in Parliament in August, the first uncrewed Gaganyaan mission, carrying the humanoid robot Vyommitra, is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. Two further uncrewed missions are planned before India attempts its first crewed orbital flight, targeted by 2027.India also plans to establish the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035. The proposed station will comprise five modules, with the development and launch of its first module already approved.The longer-term goal is to send an Indian astronaut to the Moon by 2040.Other planned missions include Chandrayaan-4, which is intended to demonstrate technologies for returning lunar samples to Earth, and a Venus Orbiter Mission to study the planet’s surface, subsurface and atmosphere.These projects form part of India’s broader Space Vision 2047, which aims to expand its human spaceflight capabilities and deepen its role in space exploration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Navami 2026: What to do with kalash water, jowar sprouts, and the end of the fast
articles.summary: By Tuesday, 20 October, the kalash on your puja shelf will have stood there since Ghatasthapana on 11 October.
articles.body: By Tuesday, 20 October, the kalash on your puja shelf will have stood there since Ghatasthapana on 11 October. The first question in many homes is: What happens to it now? Navratri spans ten days this year because Saptami Tithi, the lunar day, is present at sunrise on two mornings, giving the kalash an extended stay.Navami holds at sunrise, then slips away by iddayNavami is dedicated to Maa Siddhidatri, and it invites you to pause and reflect on what the preceding days have built in your home and mind.In Delhi, Navami Tithi ends around 12:50 PM, although some Panchangs (Hindu almanacs) may differ, and timings vary by city. The Mother Goddess's departure is observed a day later, on Dashami, making Navami the day to complete the remaining rituals. It gathers everything you have done and seals it with care.The Navami havan, or fire ritual, follows the morning puja. Kanya Pujan can also be performed on 20 October, although 18 or 19 October may be equally appropriate, depending on your family's tradition.The kalash is a womb, not a potDuring its stay, the kalash symbolises the Goddess's positive energy and creativity. It represents a womb, as does the coconut placed on top, with mango leaves arranged around its mouth. That is why it is not treated like an ordinary vessel. For ten days, you have welcomed a sacred presence into your home.By the end of the observance, tradition holds that the water inside has acquired spiritual significance. Sprinkle it throughout your house, office, or factory as a symbolic way of spreading positive energy. Let it reach the rooms where you speak, work, worry, and rest.Maintain the same reverence with which you began the ritual, carrying its spiritual significance forward. Many families do this after the havan or during Dashami Visarjan, the Goddess's farewell. Follow your household's customary timing.Closing a puja the way you opened itDo not throw used puja items into the garbage. Where appropriate, dig a small pit and bury biodegradable offerings so that they are not trampled underfoot. The end of the ritual should be as respectful as the beginning, and the items deserve thoughtful disposal after serving their purpose.What the jowar sprouts are said to revealThe jowar, or barley, sown on the first day is interpreted in folk belief as an indicator of the next six months. Well-grown sprouts are considered a sign of a favourable half-year. Small or stunted sprouts are traditionally interpreted as a sign of a more difficult period ahead and a reason to prepare.This is a household custom rather than a scriptural prediction, so take it as a prompt for reflection, not a verdict.There is also a timeline-based interpretation. Divide the batch into three parts, each representing two months. If the first third is dry or poorly grown, the first two months may be considered difficult. If the middle section is weak, the middle two months are interpreted similarly, and so on.Some people extract juice from the sprouts and drink it, considering it nutritious. However, do not assume that ritual sprouts are safe to consume simply because they have grown. Only consume them if they have been grown and handled hygienically and are free from mould or contamination. Otherwise, bury them in an appropriate place.Either way, take a moment to observe the sprouts calmly before deciding what to do with them.Which morning should you break the fast?Paran, or the breaking of the Navratri fast, has two interpretations this year:According to some local and family customs: The fast is broken on 20 October, after Navami Tithi ends and the Navami puja, havan, or Kanya Pujan is completed.According to some stricter Shastric interpretations: The fast is broken on the morning of 21 October, after the relevant Navami observance requirements have been fulfilled.These practices reflect different traditions, so the appropriate timing depends on the observance your family follows and the guidance of your priest.Ask your priest which morning your household should follow, and keep a bowl ready for the sprouts before the havan begins.Get the latest religion news and spiritual insights. articles.title: Pakistan’s decades of backing terror comes full circle as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls under emergency rule
articles.summary: Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control,
articles.body: Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control, effectively suspending the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains, which critics say has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.Decades of militant policy and blowbackPakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward. The state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark: “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authorityThe imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.Opposition crackdown deepens rights concernsThe intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. articles.title: 'Unhappy' with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's labour bill, Amazon threatens to take 5,000 delivery jobs out of the city; and experts point to what the company did in Canada when...
articles.summary: Amazon has warned it could shut down more than a dozen warehouses and move thousands of delivery jobs out of New York City over the Delivery Protection
articles.body: Amazon has warned it could shut down more than a dozen warehouses and move thousands of delivery jobs out of New York City over the Delivery Protection Act, a labour bill championed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Industry analysts caution that the retail giant is very likely to follow through on the threat if the legislation passes, pointing to a recent decision where the company shuttered facilities in Canada rather than compromise on its logistics model. The proposed legislation would mandate that Amazon directly employ upwards of 5,000 delivery drivers across the five boroughs who currently work for independent third-party contractors. Supporters argue the policy will raise wages and enforce critical safety standards across delivery providers, including FedEx and DoorDash.However, Amazon does not directly employ delivery couriers anywhere else in the US and has historically pushed back aggressively against structural changes to its labour arrangements. According to a US media report, experts warn the standoff could lead Amazon to not only pull those 5,000 contracted delivery roles out of the city, but also shut all 15 of its last-mile fulfillment stations across New York City, eliminating the jobs of 2,000 internal warehouse workers who staff them.The Canada precedent: Amazon closed warehouses over unionisationCiting logistics analysts, the report says that Amazon has already demonstrated a willingness to abandon major municipal markets rather than alter its operational blueprint. Early last year, the company permanently closed seven warehouses around Montreal, Quebec, following a union drive at its Laval facility organised by the Confédération des syndicats nationaux (CSN).By March 2025, that standoff led to the elimination of roughly 1,900 warehouse jobs and the termination of contracts for 2,800 third-party delivery drivers."Amazon will retaliate, because it has to send a firm message to the rest of the country that 'If you mess with us, this is what will happen'. When you look at Amazon's global operations, they close buildings left, right and center when there is union activity," said Marc Wulfraat, president and founder of logistics consulting firm MWPVL International.In Montreal, Amazon continues to pay rent on more than 1.6 million square feet of vacant commercial space that cost hundreds of millions of dollars to build, with at least two sites listed for sublease. Former Amazon executive and logistics consultant Brittain Ladd warned that New York City could face an identical outcome:"Amazon wouldn't blink about shutting down the 15 facilities in New York City if it felt that the legislation was a threat to its business model. This is about a model that could be copied in other cities."Amazon's delivery partners in New York City fear being wiped outThe fallout from the legislation poses an immediate threat to the 40 independent delivery service partners that employ New York City's 5,000 Amazon delivery drivers. Many small business owners say they would be wiped out overnight.DashWave Delivery owner Kris Basmagy, whose 150 employees handle Amazon deliveries across Manhattan's Upper East Side, pointed to Canada as a cautionary tale: "There was pressure on Amazon's model, and it pulled out." Basmagy added that Amazon could easily relocate distribution hubs to "warehouses being built along the New Jersey Turnpike."WGA Transit founder Joe Artus, whose firm employs 189 drivers in Harlem, actively recruiting formerly incarcerated and unhoused individuals, said the mandate would force him to shut down entirely. "I have a 21-month-old daughter," Artus said. "If this thing passes, there is no way for my company to exist or to keep my 189 employees."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
